source.title: Representational Similarity and Model Behavior in Multi-Agent Interaction
source.authors: Yujin Potter; Seun Eisape; Shiyang Lai; Alexander Huth; James Evans; Been Kim; Jacob Eisenstein; Dawn Song; Alane Suhr

record.tranche_reason: The study compares CKA similarity scores across probe datasets and CKA variants, directly bearing on the metric/data-dependence challenge in V6. It does not test convergence with scale, cross-modal alignment, or seed convergence.
record.gate_note: The study's main outcomes are multi-agent cooperation and novelty, which none of the claim versions specifies. Those outcomes are recorded as rows with versions ["none"] and summarized in fits_no_version. CKA-score correlations across datasets and variants are shown in Figure 8; the text specifically reports relatively lower agreement for GSM8K versus WikiText. Cited findings about brain–model alignment and other studies' results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study uses linear CKA between 23 LLMs only as a predictor of multi-agent cooperation and novelty. It never asks whether representations converge: no trend with scale or capability, no cross-modal pairing, no seeds, no mapping or stitching, no shared features. Figure 8 compares CKA scores across probe datasets and variants, but that checks the authors' own predictor. It does not test whether a convergence result weakens under other measures or inputs, and the text gives no numbers. The convergence claim is neither tested nor relied on; related work only discusses representational similarity methods.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that model pairs with more similar representations (CKA) cooperate better but produce less novel joint output. They report this holds across probe datasets, CKA variants, temperature 0.3, and controls for behavioural difference, performance disparity, family, tokenizer and size. The exception is KBC, where similarity loses significance after controlling for behavioural difference. Early-layer similarity is most predictive, which they read as shared lexical-semantic grounding. They caution that the relation is likely context-dependent and that CKA captures limited aspects of representations.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses CKA to relate model-pair representations to multi-agent outcomes; it does not test the original scale-convergence claim or reproduce a convergence measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: CKA similarity scores show relatively lower agreement between the GSM8K and WikiText probe datasets; the study also compares CKA variants. For behavioral associations, reported effects vary by game and novelty task.

fits_no_version.finding: Pairwise WikiText global-average linear CKA ranges from 0.106 (gemma-3-4b vs gemma-3-12b) to 0.92 (phi-4 vs itself). Within-family pairs tend to be more similar, and the Gemma family is generally less similar to other models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across current open-weight LLMs, CKA similarity varies widely and is structured by model family. Scale or capability trends were not analysed.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher CKA between interacting models predicts higher cooperation in all four games and lower novelty (uniqueness, mutual information) in most tasks. These associations hold across probe datasets, CKA variants, temperature and controls; early layers show the strongest associations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational similarity between interacting LLMs predicts higher cooperation and lower collective novelty.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study uses CKA as its representation-similarity measure and notes that it captures limited aspects of representation spaces. The text reports relatively lower agreement between some probe-dataset scores, but Figure 8's correlation values are not stated in the text. Results are observational associations between model-pair similarity and behavior, not a test of convergence as models scale.
record.rows_left_out: The appendices report further separate results for other probe datasets, CKA variants, maximum-aligned aggregation, performance-disparity controls, layer groups, temperature 0.3, and alternative mutual-information analyses (Appendix E, Tables 2–47, and Appendix F, Tables 44–47). These were not extracted individually; the retained rows use the stated default WikiText, global-average linear CKA condition for the behavioral outcomes, plus the plotted dataset/variant comparison relevant to V6.

untested.parts: No analysis of whether cross-model CKA rises with model size or capability; size difference enters only as a control in the behaviour regressions.
Language models only; no image-caption alignment.
No models differing only by seed.
No linear maps, stitching, relative representations or unpaired alignment.
No convergence result is examined across metrics, neighbours or OOD inputs; dataset and variant comparisons concern only the CKA predictor of behaviour.
No test of whether alignment plateaus or whether shared data or objectives explain it.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R3 and R4 to V6 and gave V6 a 'supports' label; both links and the label are removed. Figure 8 checks the predictor's consistency, and no correlation values appear in the text. Section 4.2 explicitly finds no difference in behavioural effect size across probe datasets. The study is better treated as using CKA as an off-the-shelf similarity tool for an unrelated outcome.

versions.untested_parts: No test of whether representation alignment rises with model size or capability.
No paired image-caption vision–language alignment test, or trend against both models' performance.
No independently initialized training seeds or shared-feature/subspace analysis.
No representation mapping, stitching, relative-representation transfer, or unpaired alignment test.
No recurring interpretable-feature or circuit analysis.

Tests dependence of measured CKA scores on probe datasets and CKA variants, but does not test whether a convergence-with-scale result vanishes under other similarity measures or out-of-distribution inputs.
Does not test whether representation convergence plateaus or whether shared training data/objectives cause convergence.
